
=================================================================
#72 Yellow Mountain  (660 August)
Arc: Part III — Kingfall / The Fall of Baekje · place: hwangsan · tone: epic last stand
Logline: Five thousand men against an empire and a kingdom. Gyebek has already done the arithmetic.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Gyebek can count to fifty thousand. He has done it twice since dawn. The answer has not improved.
[1] [MAP 660: ]
[2] ── SCENE: Yellow Mountain Fields ──
[3] ¶ Hundred-Victories gets to the **Yellow Mountain Fields** first and picks his ground. Then he waits, for the Sword of Silla or for arithmetic, whichever arrives with a banner.
[4] [PLACE hwangsan: Good ground for whoever gets there first.]
[5] ¶ He sets three camps across the three ways in. There is no fourth way in; that is why he chose the place.
[6] ¶ He walked the ground for two days before choosing it, in the same direction each time, and he can still tell you the number of paces between the eastern camp and the stream.
[7] Gyebek: Four hundred and twelve.
[8] Gyebek: …Nobody asked. I know.
[9] ¶ His adjutant is Seokdal, a ferryman’s son from the bear ferry. He has kept Gyebek’s tallies since the border and has never once been thanked for it. He does not expect to start today.
[10] Seokdal: Scouts are back, General. Over the Tanhyeon pass. Yushin’s banner in front.
[11] Gyebek: How many.
[12] Seokdal: Fifty thousand, my lord.
[13] Gyebek: And ours.
[14] Seokdal: …You know ours, General.
[15] Gyebek: Say it. I want it said once.
[16] Seokdal: Five thousand.
[17] Gyebek: Five thousand against fifty thousand….
[18] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 47, Biographies — Gyebek; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 452): With the men of one country I face the great armies of Tang and Silla, and whether the country lives or dies cannot be known…❞
[19] Seokdal: And the sea, General. Sails at the river mouth. The boatmen gave up counting them.
[20] Gyebek: Then I will count them later.
[21] ¶ Here is the man the boatmen gave up on. His name is Su Dingfang, and he is sixty-five. Three winters ago he took a qaghan’s camp in a blizzard, before anyone in it had found his boots. His regiment painted a red bird on his tent afterwards, and Chang’an calls him the **Red Fowl**.
[22] [CARD Red Fowl: The Red Fowl. Sixty-five, and he still prefers to march at night.]
[23] Red Fowl: Snow is just cold sand. / Nobody expects you in it. That’s the only good thing about it.
[24] ── SCENE: Deokmul Island ──
[25] ¶ That summer he sails east with a hundred and thirty thousand men and anchors off a small island. A hundred Silla ships come out to meet him. At their head is the crown prince, Bupmin. He is thirty-four, and trying not to stare at the size of the Tang flagship.
[26] [MAP 660: An empire crosses the sea. A prince rows out to meet it and tries not to stare.]
[27] Red Fowl: You’re the son?
[28] King Munmu: Kim Bupmin, General. My father the king sends his—
[29] Red Fowl: Tenth day of the seventh month. South of Sabi. Your army and mine, on the same field, on the same morning. / Tell your father. Tell him twice.
[30] King Munmu: We will be there, General.
[31] ¶ Bupmin is rowed back to his own ship. Behind him the Red Fowl says something to his staff that makes them laugh.
[32] Red Fowl: They’ll be late. Small countries always are. They have to ask too many uncles.
[33] ── SCENE: Geumdol Fortress ──
[34] ¶ The king rides as far as a hill fort and no farther. The field belongs to his son and to Yushin. Under Yushin ride two more generals. Heumsun is his younger brother, with a boy of fifteen in the ranks. Pumil has one of sixteen. Fifty thousand men march west with a date in their heads, and between them and the date sits a man called Gyebek.
[35] King Muyeol: The tenth day, then. / …Yushin. Don’t let the Tang get there first. They’ll write it down that way for a thousand years.
[36] ── SCENE: Final Ford ──
[37] ¶ On the ninth day, the Tang fleet sails into the river mouth at Final Ford. The shore there is a mile of grey mud. Baekje’s soldiers wait on the high ground. They watch the first Tang companies wade in up to the thigh.
[38] [PLACE gibeolpo: A river mouth made of mud, and Sabi’s front door.]
[39] Red Fowl: Mud is just wet road. / Give it something to hold.
[40] ¶ His men lay willow mats on the mud, one after another, a road made of baskets, and the army walks across it dry-shod. By evening the Baekje line is broken and the river is open to Sabi.
[41] ¶ The same morning, forty miles east, the Silla army comes down out of the hills onto the Yellow Mountain Fields, and finds five thousand men already standing in its way.
[42] [MAP 660: One army from the sea, one from the hills, and one road to the capital between them.]
[43] [FORMATION Yellow Mountain, ninth day of the seventh month, 660: 5,000 against 50,000. Three camps across three roads, and no fourth way in.]
[44] [battle]
[45] ¶ Then the air above the Yellow Mountain does what air should not. **Kangrim** hangs there in plain day — visible not to one dying man but to all five thousand at once. They have already finished negotiating with life.
[46] ¶ They cheer. They wave. Someone shouts a greeting as if King Yumla’s escort were a popular general arriving late to his own war. Kangrim, who has collected kings with less fuss for His Majesty, actually blinks.
[47] Kangrim: …You can all see me. / That is — new. / Ah. You have already decided. Of course.
[48] Gyebek: Men of Baekje — / If even death showed up early, we must be on time. / Spears.
[49] ¶ Gyebek kneels. He plants his sword in the yellow dust, point down. Inside its ring pommel sits a phoenix, the same bird that rode the incense burner he once dove for. He keeps his hand on it. Gyebek stands when the dust has learned the shape.
[50] ¶ Seventh-month heat sits on the Yellow Mountain like a second army. Dust rises white off the three roads. Downstream, Tang sails already crowd the river mouth. They are waiting for the inland door to open. This field is that door.
[51] ¶ Dust on the ridge. The Silla marshal rides out ahead of his army.
[52] Kim Yushin: So — you are this Hundred-Victories Gyebek I have heard of? / The taverns still split the Greatest Blade of Samhan between us. Shall we settle their argument?
[53] Gyebek: Then you must be the Sword of the Divine Country. / I do not drink in taverns. I count. Today the count is five against fifty — and titles after.
[54] Kim Yushin: Fifty thousand is a number. / Five thousand that already waved at death is another kind of number. / Hold your ground, then. We will come and measure it.
[55] ── SCENE: The First Clash ──
[56] ¶ Silla comes on the first time in three columns: Yushin centre, Heumsun left, Pumil right. Down the three roads at once, exactly as the arithmetic says. Uphill. In the heat. Into yellow shields set edge to edge. The archers wait to see which column is thickest, and loose at that one. All three camps throw them back into their own dust.
[57] Gyebek: One.
[58] [battle]
[59] ── SCENE: The Second Clash ──
[60] ¶ The second time Silla does not spread itself across three roads. It comes down the northern road in one fist at the left camp, hwarang in front, on the theory that the camp which shot the most is the camp with the fewest arrows left. It is a good theory. The left camp has counted its arrows too, and has been shooting half of what it could. The fist opens on the stakes and goes back up the road carrying its own.
[61] Gyebek: Two.
[62] [battle]
[63] Gyebek: Report.
[64] Seokdal: …Left camp still has arrows. / Centre has men. / Right has both, and less of each than an hour ago.
[65] ── SCENE: The Third Clash ──
[66] ¶ The third time Pumil takes the southern road, where the ground is softest and the right camp sits lowest, and for the length of a held breath the right road almost opens — and closes again on spears counted in the night. The camp is not quite where Pumil’s scouts drew it at dawn. It is further back and higher, every pace of the difference is uphill, and the Silla line arrives at the stakes with nothing left in its legs.
[67] Gyebek: Three.
[68] [battle]
[69] ── SCENE: The Fourth Clash ──
[70] ¶ The fourth time Yushin rides at the head of the centre himself, on the white horse, and meets Hundred-Victories in the gap between the camps. Both armies stop to watch two men, which armies are not supposed to do.
[71] ¶ Gyebek comes the way the border remembers him. Gomanari at full stretch, Gyebek flat along the black neck like a thrown knife. His blade lies reversed along his forearm, edge out. There is no sword in his hand to watch. That is the point.
[72] ¶ The tall Silla helm comes in at a gallop. Yushin has heard the tavern stories. He watches the hand, the way the stories say to, and reads the reversed blade half a beat late.
[73] ¶ They meet in the dust. Nobody hears steel. They hear the white horse scream.
[74] ¶ Then the white horse is going back the way it came with a red line along its shoulder, and the Sword of Silla is holding his left arm against his ribs. Gyebek turns Gomanari in his own length and walks him home. He came for one cut. He got half of one.
[75] ¶ Behind him the fifty thousand sit down where they stand. Four times up the same slope in the same heat — the clerks will write that the soldiers’ strength was spent, which is the polite way to say that grown men are lying in the dust of their own road and cannot be made to get up.
[76] Gyebek: Four.
[77] [battle]
[78] ¶ After the fourth time there is a lull, the kind both sides pretend is for water. Yushin rides out alone into the gap on the white horse, his sleeve tied off with his own sash, and stops at a distance where a bow would be bad manners. After a while the black horse comes out of the centre camp to meet him. Nobody is near enough to hear. The chronicle has it anyway, the way it has most things, from men who swore afterwards they had not been listening.
[79] ¶ Black horse, white horse, nose to nose in the yellow dust. From either line they look like a pair of go stones someone has forgotten to play.
[80] Kim Yushin: Your right camp. You moved it in the night.
[81] Gyebek: Forty paces. / …You noticed.
[82] Kim Yushin: On the third time. Not before. / …How old are you.
[83] Gyebek: Forty. Near enough. Nobody wrote it down.
[84] Kim Yushin: Sixty-five. / If we had met when I was forty, I would have had you. / …No. I would not have.
[85] ¶ Gyebek looks at the tied sleeve and does not say anything polite about it.
[86] Gyebek: You came yourself, the fourth time. You did not have to.
[87] Kim Yushin: The boys needed to see it could be done.
[88] Gyebek: Could it?
[89] Kim Yushin: Not by me. Not today. / I came with fifty thousand. I still have forty-some. You came with five.
[90] Gyebek: Four. Now.
[91] Kim Yushin: I know. I can count too.
[92] Gyebek: Then go home.
[93] Kim Yushin: You first.
[94] ¶ Neither of them laughs, but it is close.
[95] Gyebek: Your taverns.
[96] Kim Yushin: What about them.
[97] Gyebek: Nothing. They will have a long winter.
[98] ¶ They turn the horses at the same moment, black and white, as if somebody had rehearsed it, and ride back to their counts.
[99] Kim Heumsun: Brother. The Tang are at the river mouth. / Tomorrow is the tenth.
[100] Kim Yushin: I know what day it is.
[101] ¶ Heumsun looks at the slope. Then, for longer, at his son.
[102] ── SCENE: Bangul & Gwanchang ──
[103] ¶ Heumsun calls his son to his stirrup. Bangul is fifteen, near enough, and Yushin’s nephew; he comes at a run, because he has been watching his father look at him since the white horse came back.
[104] Kim Heumsun: For a subject, nothing is greater than loyalty. For a son, nothing is greater than filial piety. / To see the danger and give your life to it — that keeps both, whole, at once.
[105] [CARD Bangul: Yushin’s nephew. Young, brave, and in a hurry.]
[106] Bangul: I have heard you, Father.
[107] ¶ Bangul rides out alone and does not come back. He goes into the Baekje line where it is thickest and fights there until it closes over him, and the place where it closed is the place Silla aims at next.
[108] ¶ Pumil does not call his son. He has him brought to stand in front of his horse, before all the generals, and points at him the way a man points at a map.
[109] [CARD Gwanchang: Gwanchang. A hwarang so young they had to pad the helmet.]
[110] [CARD Kim Pumil: A Silla general with a son in the ranks. He knows exactly where the boy is standing.]
[111] Kim Pumil: My son is only sixteen, but his spirit is brave enough. / In today’s battle — can he be the mark the three armies aim by?
[112] Gwanchang: Yes.
[113] ¶ He takes an armoured horse and one spear and goes straight at the Baekje centre. He gets further than Bangul did. Then they pull him off the horse alive and bring him to Gyebek.
[114] ¶ Gyebek has the helmet taken off. Inside it is a boy’s face, sweat-striped, furious at being alive.
[115] Gyebek: Silla cannot be withstood. / If a boy is like this — what are its grown men? / Go home.
[116] ¶ They put him back on his horse and point it at the Silla line. At his father’s stirrup Gwanchang does not get down.
[117] Gwanchang: I went into their midst and could not cut down their general or take their banner. / It was not because I was afraid to die.
[118] ¶ Behind the Silla line there is a well, dug that morning for the horses. He scoops the water out with both hands, drinks, and rides back the way he came. Gyebek sends him home once. He comes back.
[119] ¶ The second time, Gyebek has his helmet unstrapped again, and looks at the face inside it for a while. He has looked at faces like this once already this week, in his own house, before the light was up. Then he does what he has to. He ties the head to the saddle and sends the horse back.
[120] ¶ Pumil holds the head up in front of the army and wipes the blood from its face with his own sleeve, so that the three armies can see whose son it is.
[121] [battle]
[122] Kim Pumil: Look at him. His face is as if he were alive. / He died in the king’s service. …I have nothing to regret.
[123] ── SCENE: The Fifth Clash · The Final Stand ──
[124] ¶ Nobody gives an order. The drums start on their own, one column and then the next, and fifty thousand men who could not be made to get up an hour ago are on their feet and shouting.
[125] ¶ The Silla line, which has failed four times that morning, goes forward and does not stop. A father’s wet sleeve is worth more than a fourth failure. The left camp goes under first — not broken so much as used up. The right holds one more breath, then folds toward the centre like a hinge that has decided to finish.
[126] ¶ On the Baekje side, nobody says five.
[127] ¶ By the fifth charge the left camp is a rumour of men. Spears shorten. Names stop answering. Seokdal stops somewhere between one tally and the next. Gyebek calls the name twice, then says the next number himself.
[128] [battle]
[129] ¶ Kangrim, who has been hanging in the day like unfinished weather, comes down to speaking distance.
[130] ¶ He reads the general's name three times across the field — Gyebek. Gyebek. Gyebek. — though five thousand throats have already answered.
[131] Kangrim: General. / Your five thousand already waved. So I ask you alone. / When you killed your family to keep your oath: was that loyalty, or terror of becoming soft?
[132] Gyebek: …Loyalty. / If it was terror, do not tell them. Let them keep the prettier word. / A magistrate sent you down to arrest King Yumla. Yumla kept you.
[133] Kangrim: …The island told you. / Living men are not supposed to finish that sentence.
[134] Kangrim: Upstairs, I asked a gardener whether the dead can be put back. / He said it can be done.
[135] Gyebek: Don’t.
[136] Kangrim: …No. I didn’t think you would want it. / I asked anyway.
[137] ¶ Gyebek turns his head toward the river road, toward Sabi, where nobody is coming.
[138] ▼ FLASHBACK 632 The bank · 강둑
    [138.0] ¶ A mudbank on the White River at night. A boy who has gone into the water nineteen times, and a prince in a grey hood with a jar he has not opened.
    [138.1] King Euija: Why do you do all of this?
    [138.2] Gyebek: I gave my word.
    [138.3] King Euija: Gyebek, would you like to serve a higher purpose?
    [138.4] Gyebek: …Do you like the name, or do you like me?
    [138.5] King Euija: …People don’t usually ask that.
    [138.6] Gyebek: Yes.
[138] ▲ end flashback
[139] ¶ The field returns.
[140] Gyebek: Your Majesty… I gave my word.
[141] ¶ He says it in exactly the same words, the way you set a stone back where it was. Kangrim closes the distance.
[142] Kangrim: Walk, then. The underworld kingdom keeps better hours than Sabi ever did.
[143] ¶ The man who counted everything finishes counting, and walks. The Yellow Mountain keeps the dust. The White River, downstream, opens.
[144] ¶ The Silla clerks count too. Twenty-odd taken alive, two ministers among them. Nobody writes down how many of the five thousand were left to take.
[145] ¶ Nobody can lead the black horse off the field. It stands over the place where he went down until the Silla grooms come at dusk with ropes, and it takes six of them, and in the night it breaks the line and goes south toward the ferry it was named for. Nobody on either side ever reports seeing it again.
[146] ¶ **The pass is open. The river is open. And in Sabi, a runner is climbing the palace steps with one word…!**
